title: Mother, grandfather, uncle
hookLine: his mother dies when he is six, his grandfather two years later, and each time someone takes him in

lines: A TRIP TO HIS FATHER'S GRAVE.
cards: He comes back from the desert a little boy, sunburned, speaking Bedouin Arabic, and goes home to his mother, Aminah. For a short while, it's the two of them.
When he's six, she takes him north to the town of Yathrib, to see relatives and visit the grave of the father he never met. With them on the long camel ride: a servant woman named Umm Ayman.
On the way home, at a place called al-Abwa', Aminah falls ill. She dies there, on the road. A six-year-old boy stands by his mother's grave in the desert, a long way from home.

teach.b: Umm Ayman brings him back to Mecca, and someone takes him in: his grandfather, 'Abd al-Muttalib, the old chief from the elephant story. Ibn Ishaq's biography has a tender detail.
The old man had a rug laid out in the shade of the Ka'ba, and none of his grown sons would dare sit on it, out of respect.
The little boy would climb right onto it, and when his uncles tried to move him, the old man said: leave him be. Two years later, when the boy is eight, his grandfather dies too.

teach.h: UNCLE ABU TALIB TAKES HIM IN.
teach.b: Again someone takes him in: his uncle Abu Talib, a man with many children and not much money, who raises him as his own and will protect him for the rest of his life. Three homes by the age of eight.

teach.h: UMM AYMAN, THROUGH ALL OF IT.
teach.b: And through all of it, Umm Ayman stayed; he is reported to have called her his mother after his mother. He never forgot Aminah.

teach.h: A GROWN MAN WEEPS AT HER GRAVE.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih Muslim tells how, as a grown man, the Prophet ﷺ visited her grave and wept, and everyone around him wept too.
This is part of why Islam speaks of parents and caregivers the way it does.
The Qur'an asks believers to be gentle with them as they grow old, and gives a prayer for them, in Pickthall's words: “My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little.”
Loss after loss, and each time, somebody opened a door.

how: Honoring parents is one of the strongest duties in Islam, second in the Qur'an only to worshiping Allah; many Muslims say the prayer of 17:24 for their parents after their daily prayers.

o: Aminah, who died on the road when he was six
'Abd al-Muttalib, the old chief with the rug by the Ka'ba
Abu Talib, the uncle who raised him from age eight

games.q: who took him in — tap the pairs.
p: his grandfather, the rug by the Ka'ba
stayed with him through all of it

s: the Prophet's mother died when he was a baby
she died when he was six, on the road home from Yathrib.
as a grown man, the Prophet visited his mother's grave and wept
the Qur'an gives a prayer for one's parents
my Lord! have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little (17:24).

games.q: you're 'Abd al-Muttalib. your little orphaned grandson has climbed onto the rug by the Ka'ba that none of your grown sons dare to sit on. his uncles move to pull him off. what do you say?
games.why: Ibn Ishaq says the old man told them to leave him be, and patted his back.

practice: Think of the people who took you in, a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a coach, a teacher, a neighbor, and picture one as they were when they looked after you. Say thank you silently, and mean it, even if they've died.
If you pray, you can use the Qur'an's words: my Lord, have mercy on them both, as they cared for me when I was little.

wordCard.voice: Mother. Umm, in Arabic. Aminah, who died on the road when her son was six, and whose grave he wept at as a grown man.

carryVoice: Your line: someone always took him in. Tomorrow, the town starts trusting him with everything. Day eighty-one, done.

sources.q: My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little.
